text: Determine if a nine by nine Sudoku board is valid. Only filled cells are checked: each row, each column, and each three by three box must have the digits one to nine with no repetition. It need not be solvable.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. So there are three independent no-duplicate constraints — row, column, and three by three box — and empty cells are dots, which I skip? And I only need validity, not a full solution?
Then the crux is mapping a cell, row r and column c, to its box. Two cells can be far apart yet share a box — like zero, zero and two, two, which are both in the top-left box.

Let me think about the cleanest structure. This problem reminds me of duplicate detection with hash sets — seen-before checks are exactly what a set is for. Here there are three independent constraints, so I keep three families of sets: one per row, one per column, one per box. I do a single pass, and for each filled cell I check all three and insert. The box index is r divided by three, times three, plus c divided by three — integer division flattens the three by three grid of boxes into zero through eight.

Here's the plan. One: keep nine row sets, nine column sets, and nine box sets. Two: scan every cell, skipping dots, and compute its box index. Three: if the digit is already in its row, column, or box set, return false; otherwise insert it into all three. Two things worth flagging. First, I check before inserting — otherwise I'd always find the digit I just inserted, and flag every cell as a duplicate. Second, the box formula: r over three and c over three each give a band from zero to two, combined as band row times three, plus band column. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. Three vectors of nine sets, then a double loop over the board. Each filled cell gets its box ID and its digit, one lookup in each of the three sets, and then three inserts. One thing worth flagging — the box ID line, r divided by three, times three, plus c divided by three. It relies on integer division truncating first, so the multiply by three can't cancel the divide. And the three sets are fully symmetric, and the or short-circuits, so a hit returns immediately without checking the rest.

Let's dry-run a box conflict: five at zero, zero; three at zero, one; six at one, zero; then five at two, two. Expected false. The row that matters is the last one: two, two maps to box zero, just like zero, zero, so box zero already holds a five, and I return false. That's the whole point of the box formula. Corner cases: an all-dot board is valid. A valid full board returns true. A duplicate in a single row or column is caught the same way. All check out.

Time is O of eighty-one, which is constant for the fixed board — each of the eighty-one cells does constant work. Space is also constant, for the twenty-seven sets. Generalized to an N by N board, it's O of N squared. One more thing — since digits are only one to nine, I could replace each set with a nine-bit bitmask in an int: bitwise and to check, or-equals to insert — dropping the hashing overhead entirely. And this same structure powers the pruning in a backtracking Sudoku solver.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: three symmetric set families for three constraints, deriving the box index as a two-D to one-D flatten, and knowing the bitmask optimization, plus the link to the solver. Good work.
